title: The First Letter to Timothy
subtitle: Pros Timotheon A, “First to Timothy”
description: Paul’s letter to Timothy, his younger colleague, left behind in Ephesus to face teachers spreading “a different doctrine”: a charge to guard the gospel and to show how people ought to live in God’s household, “the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.” Paul tells of the mercy shown to him, the worst of sinners; asks for prayers for everyone, because God wants everyone to be saved; sets out what overseers and deacons must be; breaks into a hymn to Christ; urges Timothy to train himself in godliness and let no one look down on him for his youth; gives rules for widows, elders and slaves; and warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter to Timothy?
qa.answer: A letter in the New Testament from the apostle Paul to Timothy, his trusted co-worker, whom he had left in Ephesus to stop false teachers and set the church in order (1:3). With 2 Timothy and Titus it is one of the three Pastoral Letters, so called because they concern the care of churches and their leaders. It covers sound teaching, prayer and worship, the qualities of overseers and deacons, the care of widows and elders, and the dangers of wealth.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Timothy, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names Paul as its author, and the church received it as his from the second century. On that view it was written in the early or middle 60s AD, between an imprisonment in Rome that Paul was released from, as Eusebius records, and a second one. Since the nineteenth century many scholars have argued that the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul’s death by a follower, because of their vocabulary, church order and travels that are hard to fit into Acts; many others continue to defend Paul’s authorship.

qa.question: Who was Timothy?
qa.answer: A believer from Lystra, in what is now central Turkey, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1), whose faith first lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul took him as a companion on his second journey, sent him to churches in Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi, and named him as co-sender of six letters. Paul calls him “my true son in the faith” (1:2). Tradition remembers him as the first bishop of Ephesus.

qa.question: What does 1 Timothy 2:12 mean about women teaching?
qa.answer: The verse reads, “I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” Christians understand it differently. Many churches take it as a lasting rule reserving the office of teaching and governing the church to men, grounded in the reasons Paul gives from Genesis (2:13–14). Others read it as Paul’s answer to a particular problem in Ephesus, where false teachers had influenced some women, noting that the rare Greek verb may mean to domineer and that women such as Priscilla and Phoebe taught and served in Paul’s churches. All agree that the passage begins by saying that a woman should learn.

qa.question: Does the Bible say money is the root of all evil?
qa.answer: Not quite. 1 Timothy 6:10 says, “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” It is the love of money, not money itself, and the Greek has no article before “root”: every kind of evil can grow from it. The same chapter calls godliness with contentment great gain, and tells the rich not to trust in wealth but to be generous, so that they may “take hold of the life that is truly life” (6:19).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
